verdict: OK to lend in Noida mobile/consumer-electronics assembly — back component and tooling suppliers to the EMS majors, not thin-margin assemblers; structure tightly on receivables and take monthly stock-and-debtor data.
title: Noida mobile & consumer-electronics assembly: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Noida-Greater Noida is a high-tech manufacturing hub, and UP now makes about 65% of India's mobiles and holds 55% of electronics-component manufacturing [3].** The unit buys components, runs SMT lines and assembly, and sells finished devices to a brand or OEM. Cash is made on conversion, not on the device: value sits in the brand and the component, while the assembler earns a thin conversion margin. So when a proposal lands, check what share of revenue is pure assembly versus component or tooling work; if it is all assembly, ask what stops the brand from shifting the line.

## Where cash and value sit
**Working capital is the whole game: inventory of components plus receivables from one or two brands.** Capex is line-and-building heavy and funded upfront, while the brand pays on its own terms. Collect from customer the receivable days, inventory days and the single-buyer share before you price anything. If one buyer is above half of sales, ask for the purchase order and the payment history with that buyer.

## What has changed now
**The national demand signal is strong — IIP for NIC 26 output is +19.3% YoY and +13.6% Apr-to-date [D], and electronics exports are +44.0% Apr-to-date in USD [D].** UP GST collections are +14.2% Apr-to-date against India's +6.1% [D], a genuine local tailwind. But peer results show the margin side is tightening: Dixon beat on topline while operating performance was sub-par, with the end of production-linked incentives, higher input costs and delayed Vivo JV production weighing on margins [5]. Amber and Bhagwati bets show the sector still stuck in low-value assembly with razor-thin margins [6]. The Singapore City plan near Noida International Airport (500 acres, semiconductor, logistics, data centres) is a proposal, not built capacity [1].

## Who to pursue, who to avoid
**Pursue component, tooling and packaging suppliers feeding the EMS majors, and assemblers with a signed brand contract and component localisation.** Dixon is deepening into camera modules and laptop production and has approval for the Vivo JV [7]; its Q Tech camera capacity has risen from 80 million to 120 million units a year [4]. Those supply chains are where a mid-sized Noida borrower can sit. Avoid pure assembly units with one buyer, no localisation and no component work — that is the Amber/Bhagwati thin-margin trap [6].

## How to grow safely, and early warnings
**Structure against receivables, not hope: charge on stock and book debts, monthly stock-and-debtor statements, and a covenant capping single-buyer concentration.** Take GST returns monthly and match them to sales. Watch for: receivable days stretching beyond the stated terms; a buyer cutting orders or delaying payment; inventory building without matching sales; and any sign the unit is chasing volume at negative conversion margin. If a borrower's margin falls while sales rise, ask whether incentives have ended — that is exactly the Dixon pattern [5].

## Early-warning dashboard
- Monthly GST return vs sales (monthly): gap above 10% -> ask for explanation and hold further drawdown
- Top-buyer receivable days (monthly): stretch beyond agreed terms -> seek buyer confirmation and reprice
- Inventory days (monthly): rise without sales growth -> inspect stock and cut limit
- Component localisation share (quarterly): falling -> treat as pure-assembly risk and reduce exposure
